title: What Your Anger Is Trying to Protect

reels.hook: You were given two options for anger. Both fail.
reels.hook_b: Let it out or keep it in. The research says neither.
cards: You were given two options for anger. Both fail.
Or keep it in. Carry it home.
600 students: venting while thinking about the insult made them angrier and more aggressive.
Anger isn't steam. It's a guard dog. Ask what it's guarding.

reels.visual: V2 own clip of a punching bag hanging still in an empty gym (tag bag-still), else V1 + grain.
reels.caption:
Men tend to get two scripts for anger: let it out, or keep it in.

In a 2002 experiment with 600 students, those who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who'd insulted them ended up angrier and more aggressive than people who sat quietly. And habitual suppression has its own costs.

The third option is slower: name it, then ask what it's protecting.

Which script were you given?

Evidence: Bushman (2002); Gross & John (2003). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
reels.first_comment: What did your anger guard last time? A boundary, a value, your standing, or something softer?

reels.hook: Is anger ever the right response?
reels.hook_b: Two ancient philosophers. Opposite answers about your anger.
cards: Is anger ever the right response?

SENECA
Never. Reason can do anything anger does, without the damage.

ARISTOTLE
Yes. At the right person, to the right degree, for the right reason.
Most anger is the wrong size.
Idea: Seneca, On Anger I · Aristotle, Ethics · Moodius words
Who's right? Comment SENECA or ARISTOTLE.
reels.visual: V1 flat Slate (quotes and labels read best clean).
reels.caption:
Seneca wrote a whole book against anger: whatever good it seems to do, reason can do better. Aristotle disagreed: being angry at the right person, to the right degree, at the right time and for the right reason is a virtue, and never getting angry at real wrongs is a failing.

You don't have to pick a side to notice where they agree. Most anger, in the moment, is the wrong size.

Which of them are you closer to?

Sources: Seneca, On Anger I; Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics (both paraphrased). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.

carousel_caption:
Anger has two bad scripts: let it out, or keep it in. Venting rehearses it. Suppression hides it without resolving it.

The third way is to treat anger as information: something you value was blocked, crossed or threatened. Find out what, and the response gets clearer.

Save this for after the next argument. Not during.

Evidence: Carver & Harmon-Jones 2009 (review); Bushman 2002 (experiment); Gross & John 2003. The 'secondary emotion' idea is a clinical framework, not a tested law. Philosophy: Seneca, Aristotle.
notes: Most negative emotions pull us away. Anger is unusual: research links it to approach, the drive to push toward a blocked goal. That's why it feels like strength, and why the useful question is never 'how do I get rid of it?' but 'what did it want?'

In 2002, students who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who'd insulted them came out angrier and more aggressive than students who simply sat quietly. Catharsis is one of the most repeated ideas in pop psychology. In that test, it made things worse.

Aristotle: "anyone can get angry — that is easy." The hard part, he said, is the right person, the right amount, the right time, the right reason. Seneca thought even that was too generous to anger. Both would agree most of ours is the wrong size.
